title: Understanding the JavaScript Event Loop: Microtasks vs Macrotasks
overview: JavaScript is single-threaded, yet non-blocking. How does it handle I/O, timers, and promises without freezing the UI? The answer lies in the Event Loop, Call Stack, Microtask Queue, and Task (Macrotask) Queue.
keyConcepts: Call Stack executes synchronous code to completion
Microtasks (Promises, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver) have higher priority
Macrotasks (setTimeout, setInterval, setImmediate, I/O) execute one per tick
All microtasks must drain completely before the next macrotask or repaint
detailedExplanation:
When JavaScript executes, code runs synchronously on the Call Stack. When an asynchronous operation triggers (like a `fetch` or `setTimeout`), the browser API or Node.js background thread takes over. Upon completion, the callback is pushed to either the Microtask Queue or the Macrotask Queue.

The Event Loop constantly checks: Is the Call Stack empty? If yes, it executes ALL tasks in the Microtask Queue until empty. Only then does it pull ONE task from the Macrotask Queue, execute it, re-check microtasks, trigger any pending UI renders, and repeat.
keyTakeaways: Never starve the event loop with infinite microtask recursion
Promises always resolve before setTimeout(fn, 0)
UI rendering occurs between macrotask cycles after microtasks flush

title: Go Concurrency: Building a Scalable Worker Pool with Channels
overview: Goroutines are lightweight threads managed by the Go runtime, costing only ~2KB of initial stack memory. A Worker Pool pattern limits concurrent goroutines to safely process a queue of jobs without exhausting system resources.
keyConcepts: Buffered vs unbuffered channels
Fan-out distribution across worker goroutines
sync.WaitGroup for deterministic synchronization
Safe channel closure and range iteration
detailedExplanation: Spawning an unbounded number of goroutines for incoming requests can exhaust memory or database connection pools. A Worker Pool allocates a fixed number `W` of worker goroutines reading from a shared buffered `jobs` channel and writing to a `results` channel. `sync.WaitGroup` ensures the main routine waits until all jobs finish.

complexity.time: O(N / W) where N is jobs and W is worker count

keyTakeaways: Always close channels from the sender side
Buffered channels decouple producer throughput from consumer latency
Worker pools bound maximum CPU and memory utilization

title: Rust Memory Safety: Ownership, Borrowing, and Lifetimes
overview: Rust achieves memory safety without a garbage collector through its compile-time Ownership and Borrowing system. Understanding move semantics and reference lifetimes is the key to mastering Rust.
keyConcepts: Each value in Rust has an owner variable
When the owner goes out of scope, the value is automatically dropped (RAII)
Either one mutable reference (&mut T) OR any number of immutable references (&T)
References must always be valid — no dangling pointers possible
detailedExplanation: In C/C++, manual memory management risks use-after-free, double-free, and memory leaks. In garbage-collected languages (Java, Go, JS), a runtime GC introduces pauses. Rust's compiler (the Borrow Checker) verifies memory lifetimes at compile time with zero runtime overhead.

complexity.time: Zero runtime cost (100% verified at compile-time)

keyTakeaways: Aliasing XOR Mutability: data can be shared or mutated, never both simultaneously
Lifetimes do not change how long values live; they describe relationships between scopes
RAII ensures deterministically timed resource deallocation

title: Designing a Distributed Token Bucket Rate Limiter
overview: Rate limiters protect APIs against denial-of-service, brute force attacks, and cascading failures. The Token Bucket algorithm offers the ideal balance between memory efficiency and burst tolerance.
keyConcepts: Token bucket holds up to capacity C tokens
Tokens replenish at a constant refill rate R tokens/sec
Each request consumes 1 token; if empty, return HTTP 429
Lazy refill calculation avoids running background timer loops
detailedExplanation: Instead of running a continuous background timer to add tokens every millisecond (which scales poorly for millions of users), calculate token refill lazily on-demand upon each incoming request: `newTokens = (now - lastRefill) * refillRate`. Update the bucket state atomically.
codeSnippetTitle: Token Bucket Rate Limiter with Lazy Calculation
keyTakeaways: Lazy refill eliminates background timer overhead
In distributed environments, use Redis Lua scripts for atomic token evaluation
Always return `Retry-After` header when rate limiting

title: Implementing a High-Performance LRU Cache from Scratch
overview: A Least Recently Used (LRU) Cache discards the least recently accessed items first when reaching capacity. Combining a Hash Map with a Doubly Linked List achieves O(1) time complexity for both `get` and `put` operations.
keyConcepts: Hash Map provides O(1) key-to-node lookup
Doubly Linked List allows O(1) node deletion and relocation to head
Dummy head and dummy tail sentinel nodes eliminate edge condition checks
Evict node before dummy tail when size exceeds capacity
detailedExplanation: A Hash Map by itself cannot maintain chronological access order. An Array maintains order but requires O(N) shifts on deletion. A Doubly Linked List allows any middle node to be extracted and moved to the head in O(1) time if we have direct node pointer reference.
codeSnippetTitle: O(1) LRU Cache with Sentinel Linked List

complexity.time: O(1) for both get and put operations
complexity.space: O(capacity) for hash map and node pointers

keyTakeaways: Dummy head and tail nodes avoid null-pointer checks
Store the key inside the node so eviction knows which Map entry to delete
Ideal foundation for in-memory caching tiers

title: Optimizing React Rendering: useMemo, useCallback, and Fiber Reconciliation
overview: React's Virtual DOM diffing (Fiber) is fast, but unnecessary component re-renders can degrade framerates. Learn when to memoize, how referential equality triggers renders, and how to maintain steady 60fps animations.
keyConcepts: Component renders when state, props, or parent re-renders
useCallback preserves function reference identity across renders
useMemo caches expensive computation results between renders
React.memo performs shallow prop comparison on child components
detailedExplanation: Every time a component re-renders, inline functions and object literals receive fresh memory references (`{} !== {}`). When passed to memoized children, this breaks `React.memo` shallow comparison. Use `useCallback` to stabilize event handlers and `useMemo` to cache heavy calculations.

complexity.time: O(1) render skip when props match

keyTakeaways: Don't over-memoize trivial primitives; memoization has memory and comparison cost
Always stabilize callbacks passed to React.memo child components
Use keys with unique stable IDs, never array indices

title: Python Asyncio Internals: Coroutines, Tasks, and Non-Blocking I/O
overview: Python's `asyncio` library provides concurrent code execution using cooperative multitasking and the async/await syntax on a single thread.
keyConcepts: Coroutines declared with async def return coroutine objects
await pauses coroutine execution until future completes, yielding to event loop
asyncio.gather runs multiple coroutines concurrently
Do NOT run CPU-bound blocking code directly on the event loop
detailedExplanation: Unlike OS threads which are preemptively scheduled by the operating system kernel, asyncio uses cooperative multitasking. Coroutines yield control voluntarily at `await` expression boundaries. For CPU-heavy work, delegate to `asyncio.to_thread` or `ProcessPoolExecutor`.
codeSnippet:
import asyncio
import aiohttp

async def fetch_status(session: aiohttp.ClientSession, url: str) -> dict:
    async with session.get(url) as response:
        return {"url": url, "status": response.status}

async def main():
    urls = [
        "https://httpbin.org/delay/1",
        "https://httpbin.org/status/200",
        "https://httpbin.org/status/404",
    ]
    
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        # Schedule concurrent network requests
        tasks = [fetch_status(session, url) for url in urls]
        results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)
        
        for res in results:
            print(f"{res['url']} -> {res['status']}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
codeSnippetTitle: Concurrent HTTP Requests with Asyncio and Aiohttp
keyTakeaways: asyncio is ideal for high-concurrency I/O-bound workloads
Never call `time.sleep()` inside async code; use `await asyncio.sleep()`
Use `asyncio.TaskGroup` in Python 3.11+ for structured concurrency

title: Database Storage Engines: B-Trees vs Log-Structured Merge (LSM) Trees
overview: Relational databases like PostgreSQL and MySQL InnoDB utilize B+ Trees, while high-throughput write stores like Cassandra and RocksDB use LSM Trees. Here is how they differ under the hood.
keyConcepts: B+ Tree: balanced tree optimized for disk pages with O(log N) read and write
LSM Tree: appends writes to memory MemTable, flushes sequentially to immutable SSTables
B+ Trees optimize for read latency and range queries
LSM Trees maximize write throughput by converting random writes into sequential writes
detailedExplanation: Hard drives and SSDs provide significantly higher throughput for sequential writes than random in-place updates. B+ Trees update disk pages in-place, requiring random I/O and write-ahead logging (WAL). LSM Trees append to an in-memory red-black tree (MemTable) and a sequential WAL, achieving immense write speeds. Background compaction merges SSTables and applies tombstones.
codeSnippet:
-- PostgreSQL B-Tree Index Demonstration
CREATE TABLE user_events (
    id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id INT NOT NULL,
    event_type VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW()
);

-- Composite B-Tree Index covering user and timestamp
CREATE INDEX idx_user_events_user_time 
ON user_events (user_id, created_at DESC);

-- EXPLAIN ANALYZE proves Index Scan takes O(log N)
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM user_events
WHERE user_id = 42
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 10;

complexity.time: B+ Tree: O(log N) read/write; LSM: O(1) write, O(log N) read
complexity.space: O(N) disk storage with index overhead

keyTakeaways: Use B+ Tree indexes for balanced read/write mixed OLTP workloads
Use LSM Trees when write throughput dominates (time-series, clickstream)
Always design composite indexes matching query filter order

title: Real-Time Web: WebSockets vs Server-Sent Events (SSE) vs Polling
overview: Modern applications require live data updates. Choosing between bidirectional WebSockets and lightweight unidirectional Server-Sent Events (SSE) depends on your communication flow.
keyConcepts: WebSockets: full-duplex TCP connection initiated via HTTP 101 Upgrade
SSE: unidirectional server-to-client stream over HTTP with automatic reconnection
Polling: repetitive HTTP requests wasting bandwidth on header overhead
SSE operates over standard HTTP/2 multiplexing without firewall traversal issues
detailedExplanation: If the client needs to stream audio/video or send high-frequency messages back to the server (like in gaming or collaborative drawing), WebSockets is the proper protocol. If the client only consumes updates (stock tickers, LLM token streaming, notifications), Server-Sent Events (SSE) is much simpler, supports HTTP/2 multiplexing natively, and has built-in reconnection.

complexity.space: O(1) state per active client connection

keyTakeaways: Use SSE for LLM streaming and dashboard notifications
Use WebSockets for multiplayer gaming and live chat
HTTP/2 multiplexing allows hundreds of SSE streams over a single TCP socket

title: Microservices Communication: High Performance with gRPC and Protocol Buffers
overview: REST over JSON is ubiquitous, but binary serialization via Protocol Buffers combined with HTTP/2 transport allows gRPC to achieve up to 7x-10x higher throughput with strict schema contracts.
keyConcepts: Protocol Buffers encode messages into compact binary formats
Strict contract-first schema definition (.proto files)
HTTP/2 provides multiplexing, header compression (HPACK), and bi-directional streaming
Automatic type-safe client and server code generation across 10+ languages
detailedExplanation: JSON is verbose and requires string parsing CPU cycles. Protocol Buffers serialize typed fields into tag-length-value binary bytes. gRPC leverages HTTP/2 streams to allow multiple RPC calls in flight over one persistent TCP connection.

complexity.space: Up to 80% smaller payload size vs JSON

keyTakeaways: Contract-first approach eliminates API drift between microservice teams
Ideal for internal service-to-service communication
Supports 4 communication patterns: Unary, Client streaming, Server streaming, Bidirectional

title: Dynamic Programming: Demystifying the 0/1 Knapsack Problem
overview: The 0/1 Knapsack Problem is the quintessential dynamic programming paradigm. Given weights and values of items, determine the maximum value that can fit into a knapsack of limited capacity.
keyConcepts: Optimal substructure: optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems
Overlapping subproblems allow memoization or bottom-up tabulation
Each item can be either chosen (1) or excluded (0)
Space optimization reduces 2D table to a 1D array traversing backwards
detailedExplanation: Let `dp[w]` be the maximum value achievable with capacity `w`. For each item `(weight, value)`, iterate `w` from `capacity` down to `weight`. Transition: `dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w - weight] + value)`. Traversing backwards ensures each item is used at most once.
keyTakeaways: Traverse backwards for 0/1 Knapsack; traverse forwards for Unbounded Knapsack
1D array saves O(N * W) space down to O(W)
Forms basis for subset sum, partition problem, and coin change

title: System Design: The CAP Theorem and PACELC in Real-World Distributed Systems
overview: The CAP Theorem states that a distributed data store can guarantee at most two out of Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance. In the real world, network partitions are inevitable, making the choice CP vs AP.
keyConcepts: Consistency (C): Every read receives the most recent write or an error
Availability (A): Every non-failing node returns a non-error response (without guarantee of latest data)
Partition Tolerance (P): The system continues operating despite dropped or delayed network packets
PACELC Extension: Even when no partition occurs (Else), choose between Latency (L) and Consistency (C)
detailedExplanation:
Because network cables can be cut and routers can fail, distributed systems cannot forfeit Partition Tolerance. Thus, under a partition:
- **CP Systems** (e.g. etcd, ZooKeeper, Google Spanner): Reject writes or wait for consensus to prevent split-brain.
- **AP Systems** (e.g. Cassandra, DynamoDB): Accept writes on any node and reconcile conflicts later (eventual consistency).
keyTakeaways: Partition tolerance cannot be abandoned in distributed networks
Tune quorum parameters (W + R > N) to balance latency against strong consistency
PACELC provides a complete picture of distributed trade-offs during normal operation
